aspect_adaptations: Data-format adaptation: assertions_contracts = schema-as-contract (yamllint style rules, JSON Schema / consumer schemas such as kubeconform, consumer-side re-validation); bounded_work = document bytes, keys, depth, alias count and post-expansion size bounds (the billion-laughs class); concurrency = concurrent writers of shared YAML state, multi-document stream semantics, and CI serialization via Actions concurrency groups (documents themselves do not execute); memory_ownership = parser memory discipline measured on the expanded document, streaming vs DOM loading, and the extra cost of comment-preserving round-trip parsers; static_analysis = the pinned linters/validators (yamllint, yaml-language-server, actionlint, zizmor, kubeconform).

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the specification ecosystem's own model: the YAML 1.2.2 spec defines resolution and uniqueness but leaves semantic contracts to schemas, and JSON Schema (2020-12, still the latest released draft) is the standard contract language; consumer-side validation at the boundary is the documented defense against validator/consumer disagreement.
assertions_contracts.evidence: The 1.2.2 specification (opened directly) states mapping-key uniqueness and core-schema resolution in the sections the guide cites; json-schema.org still names 2020-12 as the current version.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Schema validation is the assertion system, in three layers: yamllint (syntax/style, --strict) first, then a schema (JSON Schema, or the consumer's own - kubeconform for Kubernetes, actionlint+zizmor for Actions), then consumer-side re-validation at the runtime boundary; a document class without a schema gets one before it grows a second consumer; a document failing any layer is rejected whole.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official YAML source prescribes numeric budgets; the guide's alias bound has direct precedent in a shipping parser - the JavaScript yaml package caps alias resolution (maxAliasCount, default 100) explicitly to prevent exponential entity expansion. Stricter-than-default project bounds are policy, not contradiction.
bounded_work.evidence: The eemeli/yaml options documentation lists maxAliasCount with default 100 and describes it as preventing exponential entity expansion attacks - the exact precedent and number the guide's section 5 cites.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named example bounds per document class: document bytes (256 KiB hand-written / 1 MiB generated), documents per stream, keys per mapping (128), nesting depth (20), aliases per document (100, fan-out <= 10), expanded size <= 10x source with an absolute cap, scalar length (8 KiB); bounds enforced by the parser during resolution, not after allocation; compressed input judged on expanded size.

concurrency.best_practice: Consistent with GitHub's own Actions guidance, which provides concurrency groups to serialize runs against shared environments, and with the one-writer/atomic-replace discipline the format's tooling assumes; no official source prescribes last-writer-wins for shared manifests.
concurrency.evidence: GitHub's security-hardening guidance for Actions (the guide's Y2) is the primary source for the workflow-side rules; nothing in it or the spec contradicts the one-writer position.
concurrency.guide_position: Adapted to a data format: shared YAML state gets one writer or an explicit format-aware merge step; atomic rename makes a single write indivisible but does not make two writers agree, so multi-writer state carries a version/checksum key; deploy workflows must serialize with Actions concurrency groups - omitting one is a concurrency decision by omission.

error_handling.best_practice: Matches the specification's own failure model (well-formedness, identified aliases, resolved/recognized tags are distinct failure points in section 3.3 of the spec) and standard validator practice; no official source recommends proceeding past a parse failure with substituted data.
error_handling.evidence: The 1.2.2 specification's loading-failure-points section separates the failure classes the guide separates; the guide adds gate policy on top, which is its prerogative.
error_handling.guide_position: Four distinct failure classes handled distinctly - parse errors (reject, naming file and line), lint errors (reject at the gate under --strict), schema errors (reject whole, naming the key path), consumer errors (the consumer's contract) - with fail-closed behavior throughout; a silent fallback to a default/empty document on parse error is named an anti-pattern, and a fallback is legitimate only as an explicit, reviewed, logged document.

formatting.best_practice: Consistent with the tools' own documentation: prettier's options page documents the 80-column default the guide warns against inheriting silently, and yamllint documents itself as a linter with style rules (including key-duplicates and truthy) rather than a rewriting formatter.
formatting.evidence: The guide's citations for both claims are the tools' official pages (yamllint changelog/repo, prettier options); yamllint 1.38.0's changelog confirms the rule set (indentation, quoted-strings, key-ordering) is actively maintained as documented.
formatting.guide_position: 2-space indent, spaces never tabs (tabs are illegal YAML indentation), block style by default, flow only for short leaf collections; one pinned formatter per repository (yamlfmt in this estate; prettier where the stack is JavaScript, with print width set explicitly because prettier's default is 80); yamllint is a linter, not a formatter, and the two configs are kept in agreement; a formatter check must be idempotent and load/dump round-trips are not editing.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Matches the parser ecosystem's documented behavior: the JS yaml package's alias cap exists because expansion is where the memory goes, and ruamel.yaml's reason to exist (comment preservation) is documented to be a different, heavier processing model than PyYAML's load/dump.
memory_ownership.evidence: eemeli/yaml's options doc ties maxAliasCount to exponential-expansion prevention; the guide's parser matrix (section 26.1) records the same per-parser behavior the projects document.
memory_ownership.guide_position: Adapted as parser-memory discipline: the memory a document costs is its expanded size, not its file size (alias expansion multiplies nodes geometrically, modeled in section 38 as E ~ b^d); streaming parsers reduce peak memory only while the consumer stays incremental; a comment-preserving round-trip parser holds the token stream as well as the value and costs more than a bare loader - the right trade for editing tools, the wrong one for a hot loading path.

security.best_practice: This is GitHub's and PyYAML's own documented guidance: PyYAML's wiki warns yaml.load on untrusted data is as powerful as pickle.load and made the Loader argument mandatory in 6.0; GitHub's security-hardening doc and Security Lab research prescribe the env: indirection, minimal permissions, and SHA pinning the guide mandates; the Sept 2025 anchors changelog confirms anchors/aliases are supported on GitHub.com while merge keys remain rejected, exactly as the guide's section 26.2 states.
security.evidence: The GitHub changelog of 2025-09-18 (the guide's Y4) is the anchors source; independent Oct 2026 write-ups confirm merge keys still produce errors in Actions. PyYAML's deprecation wiki is the safe-loader source.
security.guide_position: Safe loaders only for external input (custom tags rejected, not ignored; FullLoader is not a middle ground); anchor bombs bounded at the parser; validator/consumer disagreement (duplicate keys, 1.1-vs-1.2 scalar typing) treated as an exploit shape with one dialect and duplicate rejection as mitigations; no secrets in documents; Actions discipline: explicit minimal permissions block, actions pinned to full-length commit SHAs, untrusted ${{ }} expressions reach run: only via env:, pull_request_target/workflow_run treated as privileged triggers.

static_analysis.best_practice: The named tools are the current official instruments for each surface and their versions check out tonight (see toolchain_pins); zizmor's documented audit classes (template injection, unpinned uses, excessive permissions) are exactly the checks the guide requires in CI.
static_analysis.evidence: yamllint's changelog tops out at 1.38.0 with the rules the guide configures; zizmor 1.30.1 and actionlint 1.7.12 are the versions current pins resolve to in Oct 2026.
static_analysis.guide_position: Pinned analyzer set by surface: yamllint --strict as the universal gate, yaml-language-server for schema-aware editor diagnostics, kubeconform -strict for Kubernetes manifests, actionlint plus zizmor (offline mode as the local default) for workflows; parser-behavior matrix in section 26.1 (duplicate keys: PyYAML silent last-wins, go-yaml errors on decode, JS yaml rejects by default via uniqueKeys) with the gate supplying whatever the project's parser lacks.

testing.best_practice: Consistent with the specification's conformance model (resolution outcomes are checkable per scalar spelling) and with the auditors' own test expectations; no official source offers a competing test model for documents.
testing.evidence: The spec's core-schema resolution table (section 10.3) is the oracle the scalar fixtures assert against; the guide's rejected-case list in section 31 maps each case to its gate.
testing.guide_position: Half validation, half adversarial, fixture-based with an expected verdict recorded per fixture: validation asserts resolved types (regions[0] is the string "NO"), round-trip stability with comments intact, and the reference document's cases; adversarial covers type-confusion scalars as values and as keys, duplicate keys at depth, tab/mixed indentation, an anchor bomb that must be rejected on the bound rather than by OOM, unsafe-tag documents against every shipped loader, a multi-document stream fed to a single-document consumer, merge-key documents for banned classes, and Actions fixtures (expression in run:, tag-pinned action, missing permissions:) that zizmor/actionlint must flag.

toolchain_pins.best_practice: The snapshot is current where it is checkable tonight: 1.2.2 is the published spec at yaml.org (opened directly; a 1.3.0 changes page exists in the spec repo but is not the published current specification), yamllint 1.38.0 is the latest changelog entry, kubeconform 0.7.0 is the current release line, and the actionlint 1.7.x / zizmor 1.30.x ranges contain the current 1.7.12 / 1.30.1. The yaml-language-server pin is framed by the guide itself as a reviewed snapshot rather than a latest claim; its exact latest release was not confirmed in this pass.
toolchain_pins.evidence: yaml.org/spec/1.2.2/ identifies itself as the YAML specification v1.2.2 with no normative changes from 1.2; the yamllint changelog's newest entry is 1.38.0 (2026-01-13).
toolchain_pins.guide_position: Primary target YAML 1.2.2 with the core schema; reviewed tool snapshot in section 2: yamllint 1.38.0, yaml-language-server 1.25.0, kubeconform 0.7.0, actionlint 1.7.x, zizmor 1.30.x, with the instruction to pin the versions your own pipeline uses because documentation matching the pinned version wins over the guide's snapshot.
